title: Read the deploy ticket
instruction: Open the change ticket and confirm what the automation is about to do.
rationale: An agent runs exactly what it is told, at machine speed, and it will not stop halfway through to wonder whether this was a good idea. The ticket is where somebody wrote down what good looks like: the build, the scope, the approver and the rollback. If those four things are not on it, there is nothing here to supervise — only something to watch happen.

title: Clear the window before you start
instruction: Three things on the status wall decide whether this is a safe window. Check all three.
rationale: Most bad deploys are not bad code, they are good code shipped into a bad moment. An open incident, a change freeze or a dependency mid-rollout each make the canary unreadable, because you can no longer tell whether what you are seeing is your change or somebody else's. These take fifteen seconds to check now and hours to untangle afterwards.

title: Confirm the target environment
instruction: Check the environment label on the console before touching anything.
rationale: Staging and production run the same tooling, the same dashboards and very nearly the same hostnames, and at two in the morning they look identical. The label is the only thing standing between a test and an outage, which is why it gets read deliberately rather than assumed from which tab was open when you sat down.

title: Verify environment-scoped secrets
instruction: Confirm every secret this run will use is scoped to staging — all three, in any order.
rationale: A secret scoped to the wrong environment is not an error anybody sees: the job runs, the tests pass, and a staging pipeline has just read or written real customer data with a production credential. All three get checked because it is always the third one — the webhook nobody thinks of as a secret — that is still pointing at prod.

title: Issue a least-privilege token
instruction: Take the scoped, single-purpose token and put it in the agent's credential slot.
rationale: Least privilege is not paperwork, it is the size of the hole in the wall when something goes wrong. A token scoped to this service, this action and this window means the worst a confused agent can do is break this deploy; a standing admin key means the worst it can do is anything the account can do, for as long as the key lives. The admin key beside it will work perfectly, which is the problem with it.

title: Review the agent's proposed change
instruction: Open the diff the agent generated and read it before approving.
rationale: Approving automation output you have not read is how a bad change ships with a human's name on the approval and nobody able to say what it did. Read the diff for what it removes as much as what it adds — a dropped feature flag or a halved timeout is one line, does not look like anything, and is the change that takes the service down at peak.

title: Open the canary to 10%
instruction: Turn the traffic dial to route a small slice of real traffic to the new build.
rationale: A canary works because real traffic is the only load test that is actually representative, and ten per cent of it is small enough that the failure you are looking for is survivable. It also has to be big enough to see: a canary at a fraction of a per cent produces error rates that are statistically indistinguishable from nothing, which reads as success.

title: Watch the canary error rate
instruction: Watch the live error-rate needle and commit only while it reads healthy.
rationale: This is the only checkpoint in the whole pipeline where the new build has met real users and the blast radius is still one in ten. A canary that is already unhealthy here is a full outage at a hundred per cent, and the number does not settle instantly — give it long enough to be a reading rather than the first spike of a cold cache, then commit on what it actually says.

title: Promote to full traffic
instruction: Throw the promote lever to send the build the rest of the way to 100%.
rationale: Promotion is a separate, deliberate act from opening the canary, on a separate control, because the two decisions are different: one says let us find out, the other says I have looked and I am satisfied. Wire them into a single motion and the canary becomes a delay rather than a gate — which is exactly what it turns into on the deploys nobody remembers going wrong.

title: Arm and test the rollback
instruction: Hold the rollback switch to confirm it actually fires before you rely on it.
rationale: A rollback nobody has exercised is a hope with a button on it. Test it now, while the service is healthy and you have all the time in the world, because the alternative is finding out that the previous build's image was garbage-collected at the one moment you needed it — at which point the only way out is forward, through a fix written by somebody who has been awake for nineteen hours.

title: Log the change and the agent's actions
instruction: Write the promotion, the token scope, and the canary result to the audit trail.
rationale: Months from now somebody will be reading this line to answer a question nobody has asked yet: which build introduced the regression, what did the automation have access to, who decided it was fine. Written at the end it records what actually happened, including the parts that did not go to plan — which is the only version worth keeping.

explanation: That's a standing admin credential, not a scoped token for this job. An automation only needs the access this run requires — a broad, long-lived key turns any bug in its logic into an account-wide blast radius.

That is the break-glass override, which ships a change without an approver and without a window. It exists for an incident already in progress, it pages the whole on-call chain when it is used, and every audit of this pipeline starts by asking who pulled it and why. Using it to save four minutes on a routine promote is a control failure whether or not the deploy works.

Muting alerting for the deploy window turns the canary into a decoration. The entire reason you route a sliver of traffic at a new build is so the paging system tells you it is broken before the rest of the traffic finds out — silence it and you have kept the ceremony and thrown away the signal.

That tab is the production console, not staging — it renders identically at a glance, which is exactly how a 2 a.m. mistake happens. Close it and confirm you're back in staging before touching anything.
That credential is scoped to production, not staging. Handing an automated job a secret for the wrong environment lets a test run read or write real customer data.

title: Don arc-rated PPE
instruction: Take arc-rated PPE from the cart before you approach the panel.
rationale: Arc-rated clothing goes on outside the boundary, before anything is opened. NFPA 70E rates it against incident energy in calories per square centimetre, and the boundary is simply where an arc would deliver about 1.2 cal/cm² — the onset of a second-degree burn on bare skin. Synthetics worn underneath melt into that burn.

title: Draw a correctly rated meter
instruction: Two meters are staged on the bench. Take the one actually rated for this panel.
rationale: IEC 61010's measurement categories are not a quality grade, they are a statement about where in the system a fault can reach the meter and what the instrument is built to survive when it does. A meter bought for a branch-circuit outlet at home is a CAT II instrument; a 480 V service panel with unlimited available fault current behind the bus needs CAT III or CAT IV. Picking up the wrong one because it was closer is exactly the decision this room is built to catch before you learn it the hard way.

title: Identify the circuit
instruction: Read the panel schedule and confirm which circuit you are isolating.
rationale: The schedule names what this breaker feeds and what else drops with it — the sump pump, the lab freezer, the fire pump controller. Pull the wrong feeder and somebody two floors away starts hunting for whatever just died on them, and the only handle they find in the off position is yours.

title: Notify affected workers
instruction: Post the work notice so everyone downstream knows the feeder is coming out.
rationale: OSHA 1910.147 requires affected employees to be told before the lockout goes on and again after it comes off. An unannounced outage is an invitation: a handle sitting off with no name against it and nothing to say whether the work is done reads, to somebody under pressure, as a thing to put back.

title: Set the arc-flash boundary
instruction: Carry a boundary cone out to the marked line before the panel comes open.
rationale: The restricted approach boundary is not a courtesy line — NFPA 70E draws it at the distance an unqualified bystander has to stay outside of while the enclosure in front of you is open and could still fault. It goes down before the door swings open, because the whole point is that anyone walking the aisle sees the line before they see a reason to ignore it, and a boundary set after the fact has already failed at the one moment it existed to cover.

title: Open the disconnect
instruction: Take the handle and rotate it all the way to OFF.
rationale: Opening the disconnect is the isolation itself; everything after this only verifies and protects it. A rotary handle stopped part way has not broken the contacts — it can leave one phase made up, or the mechanism parked between positions where a knock drops it back in. Drive it to its stop and watch the indicator flip.

title: Apply your lock and tag
instruction: Take your personal padlock and tag from the station and apply them to the hasp.
rationale: Your lock, your key, nobody else's. One worker one lock is what turns lockout from paperwork into a personal guarantee, and the tag beside it carries the name, the time and the work — so nobody else has to decide on their own whether this is finished or the fitter is simply at lunch.

title: Prove the meter — live
instruction: Test the meter on the known-live proving unit. Commit inside the nominal band.
rationale: A meter reading zero on a blown fuse, an open lead or a flat battery looks precisely like a dead circuit. Proving it against a known live source is the only thing that separates the two, and it is the half of live-dead-live people skip because the instrument was fine this morning.

title: Test for absence of voltage
instruction: Test every phase conductor at the work point — all three, in any order.
rationale: Absence of voltage means every conductor a hand could reach, phase to phase and phase to ground — not only the one you expect to be dead. A backfeed from a UPS, a control transformer or a mis-landed neighbour sits at 277 V to earth inside a panel already called safe, and says nothing about it.

title: Re-prove the meter — live
instruction: Return to the proving unit and confirm the meter still reads correctly.
rationale: The instrument can die between the dead test and this moment — a lead works half out of its socket, a fuse opens on a transient. Live-dead-live is one continuous instrument check with the dead reading in the middle, so a meter that can no longer read a known source has just voided everything you measured in that enclosure.

title: Apply temporary protective grounds
instruction: Install the grounding cluster on the isolated conductors.
rationale: Temporary protective grounds bond the conductors to earth, so a back-feed arriving while your hands are inside goes down the cluster and trips the source rather than through you. They also bleed off the capacitive charge a long feeder keeps after opening — easily enough to put somebody off a ladder.

title: Prove the grounds are bonded
instruction: Hold the continuity tester on the cluster until it confirms a solid bond to earth.
rationale: A clamp that looks seated is not the same thing as a clamp that is actually making metal-to-metal contact — paint, corrosion or a burr under the jaw can leave a ground cluster sitting on the conductor rather than bonded to it, and that failure is invisible until fault current needs the path and does not find one. Proving continuity at every clamp is the last check standing between a ground set that protects you and one that only looks like it does.

situation: The clipboard supervisor from the spares racking is walking straight for the disconnect. They think Feeder 3B tripped on its own and are about to close it back in.
instruction: Stop them before that handle moves. Your lock does not mean anything if somebody closes the disconnect around it.
missed: Somebody else's hand reached the handle before you did. Whether the lock actually held the mechanism open under that kind of force was never the plan — the plan was that nobody with a reason to close it ever got the chance to try, and that depended on you being between them and the panel, not on the hardware.

situation: Your lock is off the handle. Somebody has taken it off the hasp while you were testing.
instruction: Stop testing. That isolation is not yours until your lock is back on it.
missed: You carried on working inside a panel you no longer had locked out. That is the sequence behind most re-energisation fatalities: the isolation was correct once, and nobody looked at it again.

explanation: Those test leads have cracked insulation at the strain relief. Damaged leads put your hand at line potential — bin them and draw a rated set.
That padlock belongs to another worker. You never remove someone else's lock or tag: their life is on the other end of it. Each worker applies and removes their own.
You reached into an energised enclosure. Exposed bus at 480 V will not warn you first — nothing enters that cabinet until the disconnect is open, locked, and proven dead.

That handheld is a CAT II instrument — its 300 V transient rating was set for testing at a branch-circuit outlet, not for standing in front of an open 480 V service panel. IEC 61010 grades a meter by where a fault can actually reach it, and a CAT II case and lead set have no fusing or arc rating for a bolted fault behind that deadfront. Draw the CAT III/CAT IV meter instead; the wrong instrument here fails the same way a bad breaker does, in your hand.

title: Wash hands — full 20 seconds
instruction: Hold at the hand sink and scrub for the full twenty seconds.
rationale: The twenty seconds is friction time, not rinse time: soap lifts the soil and the scrubbing physically carries organisms off the skin and down the drain. Norovirus, which causes more restaurant outbreaks than every other pathogen combined, is untouched by hand gel and survives a three-second rinse intact.

title: Take the raw-poultry board
instruction: Pull the correct colour-coded board for raw chicken.
rationale: Red is raw meat and poultry. Colour coding exists so the decision stays visible from across the line under service pressure rather than remembered — and so the board that carried salmonella never turns up under a salad, where nothing downstream will ever kill it again.

title: Sanitise the board and let it stand
instruction: Spray the board and hold while the sanitiser stands for its contact time.
rationale: Cleaning removes soil and sanitising reduces what survived it — two separate actions the Food Code treats separately. A sanitiser only earns its kill claim at label concentration for the full wet contact time, so spraying and immediately wiping it dry takes the chemical away before it has done anything at all.

title: Draw a knife from the rack
instruction: Take the chef knife off the magnetic strip.
rationale: Knives live on the rack or in your hand and nowhere else. Lacerations are the most common injury on a hot line and most of them land on the second person — whoever reached into a sink, under a towel or across a cluttered board for something else and found an edge nobody had told them was there.

title: Portion to an even thickness
instruction: Slice to the target portion thickness and commit inside the band.
rationale: Even portions reach temperature together. Ragged thickness leaves the thin end dry and stringy while the thick end is still under 165 °F, and because you only ever probe one piece, the reading you write down is true for that piece and a guess for the rest of the tray.

title: Carry the portions to the flat top
instruction: Pick up the tray of portioned chicken and set it down on the flat top.
rationale: Product goes straight from board to heat. 41 °F to 135 °F is the temperature danger zone, and on raw poultry sitting in it the bacterial load can double roughly every twenty minutes — the tray parked on the bench while a burner comes up to heat is the delay that spends your margin before cooking has even started.

title: Probe the internal temperature
instruction: Probe the thickest part and commit when the reading is safe for poultry.
rationale: Poultry is done at 165 °F in the thickest part, the point where the required lethality is reached essentially on contact. Colour, firmness and clear juices all turn well before that and all three of them lie, which is why the Food Code names a temperature and a calibrated thermometer rather than an appearance.

title: Cut the heat
instruction: The pan behind you has flared. Turn the burner valve all the way to OFF.
rationale: Fuel first. A burner still firing under a pan of burning oil feeds the flame faster than any lid can starve it, and it relights the instant the cover shifts. Take the valve all the way round to its stop — a gas cock left part way round is still passing gas into the fire.

title: Smother the flare-up
instruction: Cover the pan with the lid and leave it covered.
rationale: A tight lid starves the fire of oxygen and keeps the burning oil inside the pan, which is the other half of the job. Leave it on until the pan is cool to the hand: oil still above its autoignition point relights on its own the second air reaches it, and it does that into the face of whoever lifted the lid to look.

title: Move to hot holding
instruction: Transfer the cooked portions into the hot well.
rationale: Hot holding is 135 °F or above, continuously, and it holds food rather than cooking it. Let the well drop below that and you have stopped killing and started incubating, with a four-hour discard clock running from the moment the product fell out of temperature and a bin at the end of it.

title: Run the board through the three-compartment sink
instruction: Wash, rinse, then sanitise — the raw-poultry board goes through all three, in that order.
rationale: Three compartments in a fixed order, because each one undoes the last if you swap them: detergent carried into the sanitiser neutralises it, and a board rinsed after sanitising has had the sanitiser washed straight back off. This is the board that held raw chicken, and it is the last thing standing between that and tomorrow's prep.

situation: A porter has just tipped a tray of fryer oil across the walkway behind you and carried straight on to the walk-in.
instruction: That slick is between you and the range, and you are about to walk it carrying hot product.
missed: The oil stayed where it was. You crossed it carrying a sauté pan and the second cook crossed it behind you; a film of fryer oil on quarry tile has about the grip of wet ice, and the fall that follows normally puts whatever was in your hands onto whoever tried to catch you.

situation: The canopy has gone quiet. The hood lamp is red and smoke off the flat top is rolling out over the pass instead of going up the duct.
instruction: Nothing cooks under a dead hood. Find the control, not the pan.
missed: You finished the cook under a dead canopy. Grease-laden vapour that should have gone up the duct condensed across the ceiling and the light fittings over the pass, and the flare-up that arrives one step from now had nothing pulling it away from you.

explanation: That is a water-based Class A extinguisher. On burning oil it does exactly what the water jug does. The kitchen unit is the wet chemical Class K by the range, which saponifies the oil instead of splashing it.
That is the produce board. Raw poultry on a board that goes back to salad is textbook cross-contamination — the pathogen does not care that you rinsed it.
Those are ready-to-eat greens and you still have raw chicken on your hands. Ready-to-eat food gets no further kill step, so whatever you carry across from the raw side reaches the customer alive.
There is a blade under the water in that soak tub. Knives never go into cloudy water — the next person plunging a hand in to fish out a whisk finds the edge before they ever see it.

Never water on a grease fire. Cooking oil burns far above the boiling point of water, so a jug of it flashes to steam underneath the surface and throws burning oil across the line. Cut the gas and smother it.

title: Verify two patient identifiers
instruction: Check both documents against each other — name and date of birth on each, and the hints will not tell you which two.
rationale: Two identifiers, actively confirmed against each other in front of you — full name and date of birth, read off the band and off the requisition. Bed number is not one of them, and neither is a patient answering yes to a name called across the bay: someone drowsy, hard of hearing or confused will answer to anything, and GP41 puts the matching on you rather than on them.

title: Hand hygiene and gloves
instruction: Sanitise and glove before you touch the patient or the tray.
rationale: Gloves go on after hand hygiene, never instead of it — OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard treats them as the last barrier, not the only one. They work in both directions: your hands away from this patient's blood, and the next patient away from whatever your hands picked up in the bay before this one.

title: Apply the tourniquet
instruction: Carry the tourniquet from the tray and set it on the upper arm, three to four inches above the site.
rationale: Three to four inches above the intended site is the placement, and it is a placement rather than a rule of thumb: closer than that and the band sits in the field you are about to prep and anchor, further and the venous return is not occluded where it matters. The tourniquet comes off inside a minute. Past that, trapped blood loses plasma water through the vessel wall and everything measured as a concentration climbs with it — potassium, calcium, total protein, packed cell volume. The result has already shifted before the needle goes in, and no one downstream can tell that from real disease.

title: Clean the site and let it dry
instruction: Prep the site with alcohol and let it air dry.
rationale: Seventy per cent alcohol needs its contact time and then needs to air dry; the drying is part of the antisepsis and not a pause before it. Wet alcohol carried into the vein stings sharply and haemolyses the sample, and haemolysis releases potassium from the cells — enough to have a perfectly well patient treated for hyperkalaemia.

title: Insert bevel up at the right angle
instruction: Set the insertion angle and commit inside the band.
rationale: Fifteen to thirty degrees, bevel up, with the vein anchored by your thumb below the site. Too shallow and the bevel skates over a vein that rolls away from it; too steep and you go through the back wall into tissue — or, working the medial side of the antecubital fossa, into the brachial artery and the median nerve lying alongside it.

title: Fill tubes in the order of draw
instruction: Blood culture, light blue, gold, green, lavender, grey — in that order.
rationale: Additive carries over on the needle from one tube to the next, which is why the order is the control and why ISO 6710 colour-codes the closures at all. EDTA dragged into a chemistry tube chelates the calcium and sends potassium through the roof; a citrate tube drawn late or left short breaks the 9:1 blood-to-anticoagulant ratio every clotting result is calculated from.

title: Release the tourniquet
instruction: Release the tourniquet before you withdraw the needle.
rationale: The tourniquet comes off before the needle does. Pull out while the vein is still distended and the pressure behind it pushes blood into the surrounding tissue at the puncture site — that is the haematoma the patient shows everybody for a fortnight, and the reason they insist on the other arm next time.

title: Activate the safety device and dispose
instruction: Engage the needle guard and drop it into the sharps container.
rationale: The safety device is engaged before your hand leaves the needle, and the needle goes straight into sharps — not onto the tray, not into a pocket, and never recapped. Almost every needlestick happens in the few seconds between the vein and the container, to a device nobody armed, which is exactly the gap engineered sharps protection was made law to close.

title: Hold pressure on the site
instruction: Hold gauze on the site with the arm straight.
rationale: Direct pressure with the arm held straight until the bleeding has actually stopped — longer again if the patient is on warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant. Bending the elbow over the gauze feels like pressure and is not: it holds the puncture open inside a fold of skin and fills the fossa with blood.

title: Label the tubes at the bedside
instruction: Print and apply the labels here, in front of the patient.
rationale: Labelling happens here, at the chair, after the draw, with the patient still in front of you and the band still readable. Every metre between the tube and the person is a chance for it to become somebody else's sample, and a mislabelled tube arrives at the lab indistinguishable from a correct one — the error surfaces in the treatment it causes.

situation: The patient has gone quiet and grey and their head has tipped back against the rest.
instruction: Look at your patient, not at the tubes.
missed: You finished the draw and looked up to a patient who had fainted in the chair. Most of them come round with their feet up and no harm done — the ones that do not are the ones who slid out of the chair onto the floor while nobody was watching.

situation: Someone has set a pre-labelled tube set down on your tray and told you to save time and use those.
instruction: Those labels were printed somewhere other than here.
missed: The pre-labelled tubes went to the lab. If those labels were right, nothing happens. If they were not, a result belonging to somebody else now sits in this patient's chart, and the first sign of it will be a treatment decision.

explanation: There is an infusion running in that arm. Drawing above an IV dilutes the sample with whatever is in the bag — wrong arm, wrong result.
Those tubes were labelled before the draw. Pre-labelling is how samples get attributed to the wrong patient; tubes are labelled at the bedside, after they are filled.
Never recap a used needle two-handed. That is the classic needlestick — activate the safety device and drop it straight into sharps.
That container is past the fill line. Forcing another sharp in is how the one already inside comes back out at your hand. Seal it and start a fresh one.

title: Read the rough-in work order
instruction: Check the plans: fixture count, vent sizing, and the DWV layout.
rationale: Fixture units, vent size and where the wet vent picks up all get confirmed before a saw touches the framing. An undersized vent shows up as a trap siphoning itself dry six months later, venting sewer gas into a finished bathroom through a wall that is by then boarded and tiled.

title: Close the main shutoff
instruction: Turn the main off before opening any line downstream.
rationale: Assume street pressure on every fixture downstream. The branch valve you believe isolates this run may be a fifteen-year-old gate that no longer seats, and you would only learn that at the first cut. Take the main round to its stop instead of trusting a valve nobody has ever proved.

title: Bleed the line
instruction: Hold the bleeder open until the line runs dry.
rationale: A closed main does not empty a riser. The column hangs on its own vacuum until something admits air, so the first fitting cracked becomes the vent and the whole standing head lands at once — on the floor, the tools and anything open below. Bleed it down and watch the flow die.

title: Dry-fit the DWV run
instruction: Set the vent stack, then the closet bend, then the trap — in that order.
rationale: Drain, waste and vent assembles top down: the vent tie-in and the fall are the datum everything under them is set from. The trap goes last because its weir height and arm slope decide whether the seal holds or siphons out, and neither can be adjusted once the stack and bend are welded in.

title: Fit the backflow preventer
instruction: Carry the backflow preventer from the bench to the hose bib supply.
rationale: A hose bib is the classic cross-connection — the one outlet a garden hose, a bucket and a momentary pressure drop can turn into a feed running backwards into potable supply. A vacuum breaker severs that path mechanically, which is why code names this fitting specifically rather than trusting the pressure.

title: Solvent-weld the PVC joint
instruction: Prime, cement, then hold the joint together while it sets.
rationale: Solvent cement does not glue PVC — it softens both faces so they fuse as the solvent flashes off. Hold the joint bottomed out while that happens, because the pipe's own spring-back backs it a few millimetres out of the socket and leaves a void the cement never closes. That is the joint that tests fine and weeps in service.

title: Dial a neutral flame
instruction: Adjust the oxy-acetylene mix until the flame reads neutral.
rationale: Neutral means exactly enough oxygen to consume the fuel, with nothing spare at the tip. Carburising soots the fitting so flux cannot wet it; oxidising strips the flux ahead of the solder and grows an oxide film that solder simply refuses to bond to.

title: Sweat the copper joint
instruction: Feed solder into the joint once the flux sizzles and the heat draws it in.
rationale: Capillary action drags molten solder right round a properly heated fitting unaided — heat the copper, not the solder, and the joint draws when it is ready. Chase it with the flame and you get a tidy fillet at the mouth, voids behind it, and a weep that surfaces either at test or inside a finished wall.

title: Hold the test pressure
instruction: Pump to test pressure and hold inside the band for the full test.
rationale: Code names a test pressure and a duration, and the duration is the half that catches anything — everything looks tight for ten seconds. A fitting shedding a pound over fifteen minutes will drip for years behind drywall, and the callback to chase it costs more than this rough-in earned.

title: Find the weeping joint
instruction: Look over every joint under pressure and click the one that's failing.
rationale: A falling needle says the system is shedding air and says nothing whatever about where. Locating it stays a fitting-by-fitting visual, and this is the last opportunity anyone has: after the board goes up, the same defect is diagnosed from a stain on a ceiling below, through somebody else's finishes.

situation: The main wheel has turned. Somebody down the floor has cracked your supply back open to fill a bucket and walked off.
instruction: You are across the bay with both hands full and the system behind you is live.
missed: The main stayed open while you worked. Pressure came back up behind a rough-in that is not made up yet, and the first open fitting anyone touches becomes the outlet — on a three-quarter-inch service that is roughly ten gallons a minute into an unfinished floor before somebody gets back to the valve.

situation: A thread of smoke is rising out of the stud bay behind the fitting you just sweated. There was no heat shield in there.
instruction: That is inside the wall now, not on the face of it.
missed: Nobody went back to it. Hot work fires are almost always found long after the crew has packed up: that smoulder had the rest of the afternoon inside a closed stud bay with insulation for fuel, and the first anybody knew of it was the building alarm that night.

explanation: That garden hose runs from the hose bib straight into the mop bucket, submerged. Let street pressure drop for a second and that bucket water siphons back into the supply — an air gap or a backflow preventer is what stops it, not hoping the pressure never drops.
That union is still showing line pressure on the gauge. Crack a fitting under pressure and whatever's behind it — water, or a still-hot line — comes out at whoever's hands are on the wrench.
The primer and cement are open right next to a lit torch. Both are flammable solvents sitting open — vapour finding that flame is not a maybe, it's a when.

That torch tip is inches from a bare wood stud with no heat shield behind the joint. Sweating a fitting against dry framing is exactly how a slow smoulder starts inside a wall — one nobody notices until hours after you've packed up.

title: Consult and check the patch test
instruction: Read the client record: allergy history, patch test date, previous chemical services.
rationale: The patch test goes on 48 hours ahead and the record is what proves it happened, because a PPD reaction is not a rash — it is a face that closes up in a chair on a Saturday afternoon. No record, no oxidative colour, however well you know the client. The previous services matter just as much: box colour or henna at home can react with peroxide in the strand, and the client will not volunteer it unless you ask.

title: Disinfect the tools for the full contact time
instruction: Clean the combs and shears, immerse them, and leave them under for the whole contact time.
rationale: Cleaning and disinfecting are two separate jobs: visible debris comes off first, because a disinfectant cannot reach through hair and product, and then the implement is fully immersed for the contact time printed on the concentrate. That time is the whole mechanism — a quick dip wets the steel and kills nothing, and it is the sanitation failure that actually shows up on state board inspections.

title: Drape the client
instruction: Take the cape from the chair and settle it over the client's shoulders, then set the towel at the neckline.
rationale: The cape protects clothing, but the towel at the neckline is the part that matters: oxidative dye running onto the neck stains for days and sensitises skin that has no business meeting PPD at all. Settle it so there is no gap at the nape, because that is where the colour runs when the head goes forward at the backwash.

title: Glove up
instruction: Take gloves before you touch any product.
rationale: Gloves go on before mixing, not before applying, because the first skin contact of the whole service is with the tint in the bowl. PPD sensitisation is cumulative and permanent — it builds through years of small unprotected exposures and then ends a career in a single reaction, and stylists are far more likely to develop it than clients are.

title: Mix to the right developer volume
instruction: Select the developer for two levels of lift and commit inside the band.
rationale: Developer volume is the whole chemistry: it sets how far the cuticle opens and how much natural pigment is lifted before the new colour deposits. Twenty volume is roughly two levels and full grey coverage, which is what the card asks for. Reaching for a higher volume to get there faster does not buy speed, it buys a swollen cuticle, a porous mid-length and a colour that washes out in three weeks.

title: Section into four quadrants
instruction: Part the hair into four clean quadrants — all four before you apply.
rationale: Four quadrants turn a whole head into four small, controlled applications, each one worked from a clean parting where you can actually see the scalp. Apply into unsectioned hair and you are guessing at coverage: the grey at the crown gets missed, the nape gets double product, and the timing runs from four different start times you never wrote down.

title: Apply root to mid-length
instruction: Take the tint brush and apply through the sectioned hair.
rationale: Regrowth first, because the root sits against a scalp at body heat and processes noticeably faster than the rest of the head. Put product on the mid-lengths at the same time and by the time the root is where you want it the mid-lengths have gone past it — the hot-root band that comes out of doing this in the wrong order is visible in daylight for months.

title: Process and pull on time
instruction: Watch the development and pull the colour inside the window.
rationale: Development is a chemical clock that started at the first quadrant, not when you finished the last one. Pull it early and the dye has not fully oxidised inside the strand, so it deposits weakly and fades fast; leave it long and the cuticle keeps swelling after the colour has finished developing, which is damage bought for nothing. The strand test is what tells you which end of the window you are at.

title: Rinse and neutralise
instruction: Hold the water tepid and steady, and rinse until it runs clear.
rationale: Rinsing is what stops the reaction, so it goes on until the water runs genuinely clear rather than nearly clear — residual oxidant keeps working in the strand and keeps irritating a scalp that has just had peroxide sitting on it for half an hour. The temperature is part of the job: hot water on a freshly processed scalp opens the cuticle further and stings on skin the colour has already sensitised.

title: Strip down the station
instruction: Bin the gloves and leftover product, then reset the station.
rationale: Leftover oxidative colour is chemical waste, not rubbish: it goes in the bin for it rather than down the backwash, and the gloves go with it. Then the station is wiped and reset, because the next client's service starts from whatever state you left this one in — and a colourist is judged on the chair they hand over as much as the head they finish.

situation: The flat iron from the last blow-dry is still switched on at the console, lying face down on a towel, and the towel under the plate has started to brown.
instruction: Your hands are in the jar and the contact time is running. The socket strip is at the end of the console.
missed: The iron stayed face down on the towel for the rest of the disinfection. Browned linen is the stage before it smoulders, and it was lying twenty centimetres from a jar of alcohol-based disinfectant and an open bottle of developer on the same console — the ignition source and the fuel were already touching.

situation: The client has let their head come forward at the bowl and a line of colour-laden water has run past the towel and down the back of their neck.
instruction: Stop the run at the neckline before you carry on rinsing.
missed: The run stayed on the neck for the rest of the rinse, drying as it went. That is a band of stained, sensitised skin on a client who will feel it tomorrow and see it for a week, and it is the single most common complaint a board of cosmetology receives about a colour service.

explanation: That is 40 volume. The service on the card is two levels of lift on scalp, and 40 vol against a scalp is a chemical burn rather than a faster appointment — the manufacturer's own directions restrict it to off-scalp work for exactly that reason. It does not save time either: over-processed hair has to be toned, treated and then explained.
Those shears came straight off the last client. Tools are cleaned and immersed in disinfectant between every client — a nicked scalp turns cross-contamination into a blood-borne exposure.
The iron is at 200 °C and the hair is saturated with product. Thermal styling on wet, chemically processed hair boils water inside the strand and snaps it.
That is a metal mixing bowl. Metal reacts with peroxide developer — it degrades the oxidant and can turn the formula. Colour is mixed in a non-metallic bowl, every time.

That towel came off the last client's neck. Linens are one client each and then they go to the wash, because a towel that has had colour, scalp oil and possibly blood on it is the shortest route there is between two people's heads — and it is the item state board inspectors look at first.

title: Check the hot work permit
instruction: Read the permit: area, time window and who holds the fire watch.
rationale: The permit is what turns a hot-work area from 'nobody checked' into 'somebody signed for it' — NFPA 51B requires the fire-watch assignment and the time window in writing before the first arc, because the person who surveyed the floor and the person swinging the stinger are rarely the same set of eyes.

title: Clear combustibles from the radius
instruction: Pick up the stacked packaging and carry it onto the marked clear zone.
rationale: Sparks and slag routinely travel well past where they look like they should stop, so NFPA 51B sets a minimum clear radius around hot work rather than trusting a guess. Packaging left inside that radius is exactly the kind of smoulder that goes unnoticed until the shift is over and the building is empty.

title: Cover what cannot be moved
instruction: Drape the fire blanket over the fixed conduit run.
rationale: A conduit run bolted to the wall cannot be carried out to the clear radius, so it gets shielded instead. A single spark lodging unnoticed in the insulation and smouldering for hours is the classic hot-work fire — it starts long after the welder has clocked out, which is exactly why the blanket goes on before the arc, not after it.

title: Switch on the fume extraction
instruction: Turn the extraction fan switch to ON before the hood comes over the weld.
rationale: Manganese and hexavalent chromium in welding fume do their damage slowly, well below the level that makes anyone cough, which is why ANSI Z49.1 calls for capture at the arc rather than general room ventilation. Running the fan before the arc is struck means every breath from the first spark onward is already headed up the duct instead of into your lungs.

title: Put on the full kit
instruction: Helmet, leathers and gloves — all three before the arc.
rationale: An open arc puts out ultraviolet intense enough to sunburn exposed skin in minutes and throws spatter that finds any gap in the leathers. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.252 treats helmet, jacket and gloves as one kit for exactly this reason — leaving off any single piece just relocates the burn to whichever patch of skin was left uncovered.

title: Set the lens shade
instruction: Dial the auto-darkening lens to the right shade for this process and current.
rationale: Shade is matched to process and amperage from the ANSI Z49.1 tables, not picked by feel: too light and ultraviolet from the arc still reaches the cornea, producing arc eye that shows up hours later; too dark and the puddle disappears, so you chase a bead you cannot see and lay a poor one.

title: Attach the work clamp
instruction: Clamp the return lead directly to the workpiece.
rationale: The return lead clamps directly to the workpiece, close to the joint, so the welding current has one clean path back to the machine. Let it find its own way through the bench, the building steel or a nearby bearing race instead, and stray current pits and destroys whatever conductive part it passed through on its way home.

title: Set the amperage
instruction: Set current for a 3.2 mm electrode on 6 mm plate.
rationale: Amperage is set from electrode diameter and plate thickness, not guessed at the dial: too low and the rod sticks and stubs out instead of striking cleanly; too high and it burns through the plate and undercuts the toes of the weld, leaving a groove that becomes the crack that fails the joint under load.

title: Run the bead
instruction: Strike the arc and hold your travel speed inside the band.
rationale: A steady travel speed and a consistent arc length are what actually build a sound bead under AWS D1.1. Move too fast and the pool never fully wets the joint, leaving a thin ropey cap with poor fusion; crawl too slow and filler piles up over trapped slag that becomes a void the next pass welds straight over.

title: Hold the fire watch
instruction: Stay on the fire watch with the extinguisher until the timer clears.
rationale: NFPA 51B requires the fire watch to continue after the arc goes out, because smouldering slag and hot spatter can take far longer than the weld itself to find something combustible to ignite. Walking off at the last bead instead of holding the full watch is exactly how a shop that looked fine at five o'clock is on fire by two in the morning.

situation: The fume extraction has tripped out. The hood is dead and the fan noise has stopped.
instruction: The arc is not lit yet. Put it right before it is.
missed: You set the machine and welded with dead extraction. The fume goes straight up inside your hood for the whole bead, and that is the exposure nobody notices happening.

situation: The fire blanket has slipped off the conduit run and sparks are landing on bare cable.
instruction: Put the arc down and re-cover it.
missed: You welded on with the run uncovered. A spark lodged in the insulation and smouldered; the fire started hours after everyone had gone home, which is the exact thing the fire watch exists to prevent.

explanation: You looked at the arc without the helmet down. Arc eye is a burn to the cornea and it does not announce itself for hours — the hood goes down before the arc is struck.
That cylinder is lying unsecured with the cap off. A knocked-over cylinder with a sheared valve becomes a projectile — upright, chained, capped when not in use.
The guard is off that grinder. A disc that lets go at full speed goes straight into whatever is in line with it, and that is usually your hand or your face.
There is an open solvent drum inside the hot work radius. Sparks travel further than people think and vapour ignites well below the flash you can see — it leaves the area or the work does.
Those gloves are damp. Wet leather conducts, and SMAW open-circuit voltage does not need much help to find a path through you.
